thread.title: Reporting on revenue recognition changes is still causing confusion—even for analysts - MarketWatch

author: Francine McKenna
title: Reporting on revenue recognition changes is still causing confusion—even for analysts - MarketWatch
text:
Almost all of the public companies that adopted new accounting standards for reporting revenue beginning in 2018 used a shortcut that allows apples-to-oranges comparisons for revenue and profit growth that’s causing confusion for investors—and some analysts.
The new rules are supposed to improve comparability by eliminating industry-specific accounting for revenue under U.S. GAAP— or generally accepted accounting principles, the standards for financial accounting and reporting that all companies listed on U.S. exchanges are required to follow—and implementing a principles-based, single revenue-recognition model across industries and around the globe.
However, Tesla TSLA, +1.69% and The Madison Square Garden Companies MSG, +0.42% for example, implemented the new revenue accounting standard using a “modified retrospective” method, which means they did not recast prior-period results to be comparable when shown alongside the 2018 results under the new rules.
The “modified retrospective” approach was used by approximately 85% of public companies, according to SEC filings.
Tesla’s latest earnings release doesn’t highlight the inaccurate comparison anywhere, not even when it writes that the automotive revenue increased in the fourth quarter by 134% compared to the fourth quarter of 2017. Instead, Tesla attributed the boost to a “sharp increase in Model 3 deliveries.”
The new revenue-recognition rule, ASC 606, is having a positive effect on Tesla because it changed the way it accounts for automobile sales with a resale value guarantee and cars leased through its leasing partners. The effect is a higher revenue total for the car maker starting in 2018, because the sales are now generally accounted for as sales with a right of return, rather than as operating leases.
Read: The revenue-growth rate that helped fuel Tesla’s rally relied on an apples-to-oranges comparison
Tesla does remind investors in its earnings that, as a result of the new revenue recognition rules, lease accounting now generally applies only to vehicles directly leased by Tesla without using bank partners. As a result, Tesla can recognize revenue immediately for all but the 4% of vehicles delivered in Q4 that were still subject to lease accounting
Madison Square Garden companies, on the other hand, when reporting second-quarter fiscal 2019 results on Friday warned investors that “prior period results have not been restated to reflect the adoption of ASC Topic 606 and, therefore, the company’s consolidated and segment results for the fiscal 2019 second quarter are not directly comparable to the results for the second quarter of fiscal 2018.”
See also: Madison Square Garden says Q2 earnings not comparable to year-earlier numbers
It’s not only revenue that isn’t comparable if companies take the adoption shortcut. Gross margin, accounts receivable, inventory, and net-income figures were also adjusted in most cases as companies moved to new rules on what revenue could be counted when. These numbers may not be comparable when 2018 and 2017 figures are shown alongside each other and percentage-growth figures are calculated on a year-over-year basis.
Even when companies like Apple AAPL, +0.05% General Electric Co. GE, +0.30% did fully recast prior period information to provide accurate comparison, called the “full retrospective” approach, there was still analyst and investor confusion.
On Jan 2 Apple shared news about its first-quarter services business’s performance in a letter to shareholders, projecting that it generated about $10.8 billion in revenue, a number that was above analyst expectations. However, the company did not remind analysts that the number was calculated using the new revenue recognition rules. Apple started reporting under the new rules on October 1, one of the latest big companies to adopt the new rules given its late 2018 fiscal year-end of Sept 30.
Read also: Apple cuts holiday sales forecast on iPhone and China weakness, stock falls 8%
Some analysts assumed Apple’s letter was applying the old accounting standard, even though the company had told them more than once about the change—for example during its November earnings call and in the company’s 2018 annual report, as well as disclosing the potential impact in several quarterly reports before that.
Madison Square Garden did what it could to point investors and analysts to an explanation for the lack of comparability and to additional information that might make up for it.
Instead of recasting prior-year information under the new rules, Madison Square Garden followed the approach suggested by the Financial Accounting Standards Board, the accounting standard setters, and endorsed by the SEC that instead shows current quarter information as if the revenue recognition changes had never occurred.
That’s backward, said one expert.
“The Financial Accounting Standards Board created a transition method that trades off comparability for ease of implementation,” Paul Chaney, the E. Bronson Ingram professor of accounting at Vanderbilt University told MarketWatch back in August.
“The resulting lack of comparability violates an important objective of the new standard — comparability,” said Chaney.

Francine McKenna Francine McKenna is a MarketWatch reporter based in Washington, covering financial regulation and legislation from a transparency perspective. She has written about accounting, audit, fraud and corporate governance for publications including Forbes, the Financial Times, Accountancy and the American Banker. McKenna had 30 years of experience at banks and professional-services firms, including at PwC and KPMG, before becoming a full-time writer.
